stories.summary: After Chernobyl, many people explained the disaster away as Soviet stupidity: an authoritarian system where people afraid of being sent to Siberia kept making wrong decisions. Liberal democracies, the thinking went, would make better decisions. Then Fukushima happened in 2011. Angela Merkel, who holds a PhD in chemistry and can reason about probabilities, called a meeting built around one sentence: the Japanese are as good as us. Germany saw itself as better at engineering than the Soviets, but not better than the Japanese. That reasoning led Germany to shut down all its nuclear power, which Ajay, looking back from 2024, thinks was not a great decision.
stories.insight: Fukushima broke the comforting idea that nuclear accidents only happen under bad regimes. Even a scientifically trained leader reacted by asking 'are we like them?' instead of asking what the risks actually were.
stories.quote: She said, The Japanese are as good as us.

stories.topic: The Battle of the Atlantic and the Assembly-Line Ship
stories.summary: In 1941 German U-boats were sinking the ships that carried food and military supplies from America to Britain, hundreds of them, hoping to starve the island out. The Allies responded by mass-producing a plain British design nicknamed the 'ugly duckling', a ship of about 10,000 tons. Until then ships had been built by hand, each one a bit different. The Americans built them Henry Ford style on assembly lines at 18 shipyards. As the yards learned, building time fell from 270 days to 35 days. About 2,700 ships were built and costs fell sharply. American factories could make ships faster than German submarines could sink them.
stories.insight: Industrial scale plus learning by repetition beats handcrafted quality. Ajay uses this as the model for nuclear power: stop building one-off giant reactors and start mass-producing small ones.
stories.quote: what you get out of this is the gains from industrialization also very importantly, the gains from learning. As you do this over and over, the processes get better.

stories.summary: Germany's Tiger tank was excellent, but it was built by master craftsmen and its design changed after every eleven tanks produced, which pushed costs up. The Americans mass-produced Sherman tanks in factories, taught the Soviets to do the same with the T-34, and outproduced German manufacturing roughly tenfold.
stories.insight: Craftsmanship becomes a weakness when the real goal is volume and low cost. The same reasoning applies to nuclear reactors, where every component should be mass-produced.
stories.quote: Every eleven tiger tanks that were produced, there would be a change in the design. Because the people making those tanks were master craftsmen.

stories.topic: Fear Has a Body Count Too: 9/11 and Fukushima
stories.summary: Amit recalls hearing that after 9/11, tighter security and fear led Americans to drive more and fly less, and overall mortality went up because cars are far deadlier than planes. Before recording, Ajay had pointed out a similar effect at Fukushima: deaths followed when the reactor was shut down and the region switched to coal.
stories.insight: Avoiding a technology does not mean avoiding risk. It means taking on the risks of whatever replaces it. Refusing nuclear power has costs that nobody counts.
stories.quote: after nine eleven, when security measures went up and people were also scared, they started driving more and flying less, and because of that mortality went up.

stories.summary: India tested a nuclear device in 1974 without help from anyone else. Most nuclear powers got leaked knowledge: the Soviets stole secrets from the Manhattan Project, then passed them to China, and China passed them to North Korea and Pakistan. Ajay credits Homi Bhabha, Raja Ramanna, Sethna and others. But he argues that building cheap, efficient nuclear electricity is a different kind of problem, closer to running Bharat Heavy Electricals, and the Indian state is not suited to it.
stories.insight: Being good at strategic science does not mean being good at industrial economics. India's pride in its bomb has led it to treat civilian nuclear energy as a government-only domain.
stories.quote: India is one of the few countries which figured this out entirely alone.

stories.topic: Early Doubts at the Ministry of Finance
stories.summary: While at the Ministry of Finance, Ajay began early calculations on India's government-run nuclear plants. He concluded that once costs were measured correctly, they could never play a meaningful role in India's energy mix. The top reactors built by the French and the Americans were far more cost-efficient. Nuclear's share of Indian energy has stayed tiny and has not grown.
stories.insight: The government-monopoly approach to Indian nuclear power has already been tested for decades, and the result is a very small share of the energy mix.
stories.quote: I remember when I was at the Ministry of Finance. I had started on some early calculations that this isn't going anywhere.

stories.topic: Meta and Google Order Small Reactors
stories.summary: Amit praises the timing of Ajay's article with Akshay Jaitly on nuclear energy in India. It came out in practically the same week that Meta and Google placed big orders for small modular reactors.
stories.insight: When very large private buyers commit real money, a technology has moved from theory to market, and scale starts to look possible.
stories.quote: So we are beyond the world of theory. Shit is happening, orders have been placed for them

recommendations.item: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
recommendations.creator: Joshua S Goldstein, Staffan A Qvist & Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Mentioned in Amit's opening argument for nuclear energy, as a New York Times piece co-written by Steven Pinker.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the data behind his claims: nuclear's safety record against coal, France's experience, and why taking climate change seriously means taking nuclear seriously.

recommendations.creator: HBO
recommendations.context: Came up while explaining why people initially blamed Chernobyl on the Soviet system.
recommendations.reason: It shows how a big oppressive state inevitably fails, which makes Chernobyl a story about authoritarianism rather than about nuclear power.

recommendations.creator: Adam Higginbotham
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes next to the HBO series. It was not discussed on air.
recommendations.reason: Further reading on the disaster that the episode treats as a failure of an oppressive state rather than of nuclear technology.

recommendations.item: Atomic State: Big Science In Twentieth-century India
recommendations.creator: Jahnavi Phalkey
recommendations.context: A 'mid-episode recommendation' prompted by the mention of Homi Bhabha, then repeated at the end.
recommendations.reason: An excellent book that tells the story of the early pioneers of nuclear science in India.

recommendations.context: Praised in the intro and recommended again at the end. Amit's nuclear rant at the end of that episode led to this one.

recommendations.reason: It is the written version of the episode's policy case, including the five things India must change so private players can choose nuclear.

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Is the Safest Form of Energy
core_ideas.explanation: Three Mile Island killed no one. Fukushima's deaths came from the tsunami and a hurried evacuation. Chernobyl's toll is disputed. Even on the worst estimate, sixty years of nuclear power have killed fewer people than a month of coal-related accidents. France gets about 71% of its power from nuclear with no safety problems. Sixty years of nuclear waste could fit in an underground bunker the size of a Walmart.
core_ideas.quote: Nuclear energy is the safest form of energy known to man.

core_ideas.concept: Compare Deaths per Megawatt-Hour, Not Headlines
core_ideas.explanation: Energy choices trade one risk for another, so count excess deaths per unit of energy produced. Coal is the dirtiest option on pollution, carbon and safety, and by this measure nuclear wins. People misjudge this the way they misjudge flying versus driving. Flying from Bombay to Delhi is far safer than driving, but plane crashes make headlines and car crashes don't, and that distorts how people reason about probability.
core_ideas.quote: We will add nuclear risk to the world and we will reduce coal risk in the world.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay names three real problems: radioactive material spreads for thousands of kilometres, a runaway chain reaction can melt deep into the ground, and complex systems turn small human errors into big failures. All three famous accidents involved first-generation designs. Newer reactors shut themselves down when something goes wrong, with forces like gravity pulling the fissile material apart. He compares this to cars: Ralph Nader's 1965 book 'Unsafe at Any Speed' was followed by revolutionary gains in car safety, not by giving up on cars.
core_ideas.quote: This is the heart of the idea that it's about clever engineering.

core_ideas.concept: Chernobyl Was a Failure of an Oppressive State
core_ideas.explanation: Chernobyl's chain of bad decisions came from a system where people feared being sent to Siberia and so did not speak up. Engineering ability combined with freedom to dissent, debate and criticise produces good safety outcomes, which is why the Soviet case tells us little about nuclear power in open societies.
core_ideas.quote: how a big oppressive state inevitably fails. Nothing to do with nuclear power.

core_ideas.concept: Naval Reactors Prove It Can Be Done
core_ideas.explanation: Aircraft carriers and submarines rely on onboard nuclear reactors, and advanced economies have run them for decades with excellent safety records. This is large-scale working evidence across many countries, not a hypothetical.
core_ideas.quote: We have thousands and thousands of man hours of flawless operation happening every year on a large scale across many countries

core_ideas.explanation: In the 1970s the peace and environmental movements lumped nuclear power together with nuclear bombs. Amit argues that ideological tribes adopt a whole bundle of dogmas and defend all of it even when the facts change. The result is environmentalists who say climate change is a great problem of our time yet reject one of the best tools against it, which he calls cognitive dissonance.
core_ideas.quote: how ideological tribes form is that they will take a package of dogmatic assertions and then they will stick to the entire package. You're not allowed to dissent even if the facts change

core_ideas.concept: Industrialize the Reactor: Small Modular Reactors
core_ideas.explanation: Large 4,000 MW plants take about twenty years to build and only a handful will ever be made, so costs stay high. Making 50 to 100 MW reactors instead means you could build thousands, with mass-produced parts and assembly lines. The aim is a truck-sized, self-contained unit that is delivered, installed and switched on like a factory's diesel generator, with no construction project. Solar's huge cost collapse came the same way, from two simple, scalable manufacturing steps. A 50 MW plant could power roughly 25,000 households or a large factory.
core_ideas.quote: How do you get the price of a nuclear reactor down? The answer is industrialization.

core_ideas.concept: The Grid Is the Choke Point
core_ideas.explanation: The grid works like highways (transmission) and narrow lanes (distribution) carrying power from producers to users. In many Indian states it is badly broken because of how the public sector has run it. So new solar, wind and possibly nuclear projects are happening business to business, either for a company's own use or sold directly to another large company.
core_ideas.quote: That will indeed be a choke point.

core_ideas.concept: Separate the Bomb from the Power Plant
core_ideas.explanation: Twenty-four countries run nuclear power without having built bombs. Steel used for artillery belongs to defence, which cares about owning its supply chain, but steel used for power plants is ordinary global trade. Civilian nuclear energy should be treated like generation equipment from Bharat Heavy Electricals, which competes with imports, and not as a Department of Atomic Energy monopoly.
core_ideas.quote: There are twenty four countries in the world which have nuclear power, but they haven't built nuclear bombs. These are completely separate things.

core_ideas.concept: Keep the Indian State Out of Business
core_ideas.explanation: Building reactors is a business, and so is running them. Companies such as L&T, Tata Power or Reliance Energy, or a heavy energy user like Hindalco, should decide for themselves whether to make or buy reactors. The state's role should be limited to genuine market failures.
core_ideas.quote: It is congenitally not possible for the Indian State to do anything efficiently.

core_ideas.concept: The Evening Peak: A Bet Between Storage and Nuclear
core_ideas.explanation: Solar is unbeatable on price during the day, but it disappears in the evening just as demand jumps when people get home. If coal is phased out, evening prices will spike. Investors who think storage can handle the peak should build storage. Those who doubt it should build nuclear, which keeps running at night. These should be private bets, not central planning.
core_ideas.quote: But the sun has an unpleasant habit of setting every evening.

core_ideas.concept: Five Conditions for Nuclear Freedom in India
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's list for the Indian state: (1) let private Indians import nuclear plants; a 50 MW plant costs roughly $200 to 300 million, affordable for India's top 100 companies. (2) Let plant owners sell power directly to private buyers, bypassing reluctant DISCOMs, as offshore wind can. (3) Have the government protect uranium and waste the way the CISF secures private airports, paid for by operators. (4) Sign up to and follow IAEA standards for the whole fuel cycle so the world will sell India fuel and reactors. (5) Fix civil nuclear liability.
core_ideas.quote: these are the five pieces that need to be changed to create conditions for Indian private people to choose.

core_ideas.concept: Liability Should Rest with the Operator
core_ideas.explanation: Indian law holds the reactor vendor liable forever, so foreign vendors refuse to sell. The international approach works like owning a car: once the reactor is handed over, the operator alone is liable to victims. The operator can then sue the vendor if a design flaw caused the accident.
core_ideas.quote: as long as the Indian law is structured in the way it is today, there will be no transactions.

core_ideas.concept: An Argument for Freedom, Not for Action
core_ideas.explanation: The hosts do not tell companies to invest in nuclear or the state to build it, and they do not want a central plan such as 5,000 MW of nuclear. They only want the state to stop blocking the option, so private players can decide based on their own judgement.
core_ideas.quote: We are not arguing for action. We are arguing for freedom

core_ideas.concept: Invisible Infrastructure and the Homeostatic Fix
core_ideas.explanation: Amit worries that India lacks the invisible infrastructure, such as rule of law and long-tested processes, that makes Western policy designs work. Any state role could turn into cronyism, incompetence or rent-seeking. Ajay replies that there is no smooth path. The government will keep overshooting one way or the other, and a lively community of thinkers and critics is what pulls it back.
core_ideas.quote: The answer lies in knowledge and community that we need enough people in India who think, who write, who debate, who criticize.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The opening: three people at a conference called Ajay 'Amit'. He messaged Amit, 'Do people call you Ajay?' Amit replied: 'No, bro, uh never happened to me, must be something with you,' and added, 'I do kinda look like an Amit.'

Amit's twist on safety regulation: if the government really regulated on safety grounds, 'they would immediately mandate that they get nuclear power. Because it is far safer than any other kind of power in use now.'
Ajay, before his WWII story: 'all the great stories of the world begin at the second world war.'
Ajay's description of the SMR dream: 'you just go buy an SMR off the shelf from uh D Mart and you will plop it in your backyard and you've got a nuclear reactor up and running.'

Amit, after Ajay's case for industrialization: 'We are both artisans. If not artists, we can have um you know delusions about that,' so it's ironic that Ajay is arguing against doing things the artisanal way.

Ajay's back-of-the-envelope maths: a household uses two to three thousand watts, but 'between friends, I'm gonna call it a thousand,' to keep the mental arithmetic simple. Amit then sizes a 50 MW plant in Mumbai terms: not Andheri size, maybe Varsova size, 'definitely Yari Road side size.'
Ajay says the sun 'has an unpleasant habit of setting every evening.' Amit corrects him pedantically in Hindi: 'Sunset nahi ho raha, hum ghoom rahe' (the sun isn't setting, we're the ones rotating).

Amit says Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe 'have in fact been compared to our crew, Nomsita Haritashya and Vaishnav Vyas, as these photographs will indicate. Is there a similarity or not? I leave it to you to decide, gentle readers.'
The closing: inspired by 'Wherever I Lay My Hat', Amit asks Ajay where his spiritual and intellectual home is. The answer: 'Bandra East.'

During the U-boat story, Bob Dylan comes up ('there's a Bob Dylan song about this'), followed by a mock 'Blowin' in the Wind' lyric about how many ships must be shot down before the British have no food.
Ralph Nader's 1965 book 'Unsafe at Any Speed', which exposed car safety problems in the US, is used to argue that a known hazard leads to better engineering, not to abandoning the technology.

Henry Ford-style assembly lines, the American Sherman tank and the Soviet T-34 against Germany's handcrafted Tiger tank: the WWII production contest Ajay uses as the template for mass-produced reactors.
